Cloud Storage Trash

If you use Google Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive, or iCloud, deleted files often sit in a “Trash” or “Bin” folder for 30 days. Log into your cloud account, navigate to the trash, and restore the file. Google Drive even keeps files for 30 days after you empty the trash—sometimes longer for Google Workspace accounts.

Real example: A friend accidentally deleted his entire wedding album from Google Photos. He panicked for two days before remembering Google Photos has its own Trash folder with a 60-day retention period. All 400 photos were restored in five minutes.

Method 2: Use Free Recovery Software (No Scams)

If the obvious methods fail, free recovery software is your next best bet. But beware: the internet is full of “free” tools that install malware or demand payment after scanning. Stick with these reputable options.

Recuva (Windows Only)

Recuva is the gold standard for free Windows recovery. It’s lightweight, effective, and has a portable version you can run from a USB drive (no installation needed—important to avoid overwriting your deleted files).

How to use Recuva:

  1. Download Recuva from the official Piriform website (not a third-party download site).
  2. Run the wizard. Select the file type (pictures, documents, videos, or “All Files”).
  3. Choose the location where the file was stored (specific folder, whole drive, or “I’m not sure”).
  4. Click “Scan.” Deep scan takes longer but finds more files.
  5. Review the results. Files with a green circle are recoverable. Yellow means partially recoverable. Red means gone.
  6. Select the files and click “Recover.” Save them to a different drive—never the same one.

Limitation: Recuva struggles with SSD drives that have TRIM enabled, but it’s still worth trying.

PhotoRec (Windows, Mac, Linux)

PhotoRec is not pretty. It runs in a command-line interface with no fancy graphics. But it’s incredibly powerful and completely free, developed by the same team behind TestDisk. It recovers files by scanning raw data on the drive, ignoring the file system entirely.

When to use PhotoRec: When Recuva fails or when you need to recover files from a formatted or corrupted drive.

How to use it: Download the TestDisk package from cgsecurity.org. Run PhotoRec.exe, select your drive, choose the file types you want to recover, and specify an output folder. The process takes time but often finds files other tools miss.

Disk Drill (Mac, with Free Trial)

Disk Drill for Mac offers a free preview feature that shows you exactly which files are recoverable before you pay. On Windows, the free version recovers up to 500 MB. For most document recovery needs, that’s plenty.

Method 3: When to Use Paid Recovery Software

Free software works for most accidental deletions, but it has limits. If you’re recovering from a formatted drive, a corrupted partition, or a failed drive, paid tools offer advanced features like:

  • RAID recovery (for multi-drive setups)
  • Disk imaging (creates a bit-for-bit copy of a failing drive)
  • Advanced file carving (reconstructs files from fragments)

Top paid options:

  • EaseUS Data Recovery Wizard: User-friendly, supports all file types, recovers from crashed computers. $69.95/month but often has discounts.
  • Stellar Data Recovery: Excellent for hard drive failures and formatted drives. $49.99/year.
  • R-Studio: Overkill for most users but the gold standard for IT professionals. $79.99 for a single license.

When NOT to pay: If you only need to recover a few documents or photos, free tools will do the job. Don’t spend money unless you’ve confirmed free tools can’t find your files.

Method 4: Recover Deleted Files on Smartphones

Android

Android phones don’t have a Recycle Bin by default, but most manufacturers include one in the Gallery or Files app. Check:

  • Google Photos: Open the app, tap “Library” > “Trash.” Files stay for 60 days.
  • Samsung Gallery: Open Gallery, tap the three dots, select “Recycle Bin.” Files stay for 30 days.
  • Files by Google: Open the app, tap “Trash.” Files stay for 30 days.

If the file isn’t in any trash folder, use DiskDigger (free, no root required). It scans your phone’s internal storage and SD card for deleted photos and documents. Rooted phones get deeper scanning capabilities.

iPhone

iOS has a “Recently Deleted” album in the Photos app that keeps deleted photos and videos for 30 days. For documents, check:

  • Files app: Tap “Browse” > “Recently Deleted” (if visible).
  • iCloud Drive: Log into iCloud.com, go to “Settings” > “Restore Files” (bottom of the page). iCloud keeps deleted files for 30 days.

If the file is gone from all these places, you’ll need a computer-based tool like iMazing or PhoneRescue. These can scan iPhone backups (local or iCloud) and extract deleted files. They cost around $50 but work reliably.

What NOT to Do (Common Mistakes That Kill Recovery)

I’ve watched people destroy their chances of recovery with these mistakes. Don’t be that person.

Don’t Install Recovery Software on the Same Drive

If you deleted a file from your C: drive, don’t download and install Recuva onto C:. That installation process writes new data to the drive, potentially overwriting your deleted file. Instead:

  • Download the software on another computer and transfer it via USB.
  • Or use a portable version that runs from a USB stick.

Don’t Run Disk Cleanup or Defragmentation

Disk Cleanup and defrag tools permanently erase “free space.” On an HDD, defragmenting physically moves data around, destroying any chance of recovery. On an SSD, the TRIM command already complicates recovery—don’t make it worse.

Don’t Format the Drive

Formatting a drive doesn’t erase data, but it does reset the file system. This makes recovery more complex and often requires paid software. If you accidentally formatted a drive, stop using it immediately and use a tool like TestDisk to restore the partition.

Prevention: The Best Recovery Is Backup

You’ve recovered your file. Congratulations. Now do yourself a favor and set up a backup system so you never have to do this again.

The 3-2-1 Rule:

  • 3 copies of your data
  • 2 different storage types (e.g., external hard drive + cloud)
  • 1 copy offsite (cloud or a friend’s house)

Practical setup for most people:

  1. Automatic cloud backup: Google Drive, OneDrive, or iCloud. Set it to sync your Documents, Desktop, and Photos folders. Cost: $2-$10/month.
  2. Local backup: An external SSD (1TB costs around $60). Use Windows Backup or Time Machine to create weekly backups.
  3. Critical files only: A secondary cloud service like Backblaze ($7/month, unlimited storage) for full-drive backup.

Real example: After recovering his wedding album, my friend bought a 2TB external drive and set up automatic Google Photos backup. He now jokes that his “disaster fund” is better spent on storage than recovery software.

Final Thoughts

Recovering deleted files is almost always possible if you act quickly and use the right tools. The average person can recover 90% of their files using free software and cloud trash folders. The remaining 10%—usually from formatted or physically damaged drives—may require paid tools or professional services.

But the real lesson here isn’t about recovery. It’s about building habits that make recovery unnecessary. Set up automatic backups today. It takes 15 minutes and saves you from the gut-wrenching feeling of watching a file disappear forever.

And if you’re reading this because you’ve already deleted something important—breathe. Stop using the device. Follow the methods above in order. You’ve got a better chance than you think.

item.title: How to Build a PC: A Step-by-Step Guide for Beginners
item.description: Learn how to build a PC from scratch with this practical guide. Covers part selection, assembly, cable management, and first boot—no fluff, just results.
item.content:encoded:
TITLE: How to Build a PC: A Step-by-Step Guide for Beginners DESCRIPTION: Learn how to build a PC from scratch with this practical guide. Covers part selection, assembly, cable management, and first boot—no fluff, just results. TAGS: build a PC, PC building guide, DIY computer, gaming PC build, PC assembly tutorial

Introduction

I still remember the first time I pressed the power button on a PC I built myself. Nothing happened. No fans spun, no lights flickered—just silence. I had forgotten to flip the switch on the power supply. After a moment of panic, I fixed it, and the machine roared to life. That feeling? It’s addictive.

Building your own PC isn’t just about saving money (though you often do). It’s about control. You choose every part, from the CPU to the case fans. You know exactly what’s inside your machine, and you can upgrade it piece by piece instead of buying a whole new system every few years. Plus, it’s genuinely satisfying.

This guide assumes you’re starting from zero. I’ll walk you through every step—from picking parts to that first boot screen—without the marketing fluff or unnecessary jargon. Let’s get your hands dirty.

Step 1: Define Your Build’s Purpose

Before you spend a single dollar, ask yourself: What will this PC actually do?

  • Gaming at 1080p/1440p? Focus on a strong GPU (graphics card) and a mid-range CPU. You don’t need a top-tier processor for most games.
  • Video editing or 3D rendering? Prioritize a CPU with many cores (like an AMD Ryzen 7 or Intel Core i7) and at least 32GB of RAM.
  • General productivity (web, office, light editing)? A budget build with an integrated GPU (like an AMD Ryzen 5 5600G) will save you money and still feel snappy.

Real example: My friend wanted a PC for Fortnite and schoolwork. He almost bought a $1,500 prebuilt with a flashy RGB case. Instead, we built a $900 machine with a Ryzen 5 5600X and an RTX 3060. It runs the same games at higher settings, and he saved $600.

Define your use case first. Everything else follows.

Step 2: Choose Your Components (The Core 7)

You only need seven main parts to build a PC. Here’s what each does and how to pick them wisely.

CPU (Central Processing Unit)

The brain of the operation. For most builders, the choice comes down to AMD or Intel. As of 2025:

  • AMD Ryzen 5/7 – Great for multitasking and value. The AM5 platform supports future upgrades.
  • Intel Core i5/i7 – Strong single-core performance for gaming. The LGA1700 socket is mature and stable.

Actionable tip: Don’t overspend on a CPU you won’t utilize. A Ryzen 5 7600 is plenty for 95% of gamers. Put that extra money into a better GPU.

GPU (Graphics Card)

This handles all visuals. If you’re gaming, this is your most important component.

  • Budget: NVIDIA RTX 4060 or AMD RX 7600 – great for 1080p.
  • Mid-range: RTX 4070 Super or RX 7800 XT – handles 1440p smoothly.
  • High-end: RTX 4080 Super or RX 7900 XTX – for 4K or high refresh rates.

Warning: Avoid buying a GPU used from unknown sellers unless you can test it. Counterfeit cards exist, and mining cards can fail early.

Motherboard

The backbone that connects everything. Key considerations:

  • Form factor: ATX (full-size), Micro-ATX (smaller, fewer slots), or Mini-ITX (tiny, expensive).
  • Socket compatibility: Must match your CPU (e.g., AM5 for Ryzen 7000 series, LGA1700 for Intel 12th-14th gen).
  • Features: Do you need Wi-Fi built-in? How many USB ports? M.2 slots for fast SSDs?

Pro tip: A B650 motherboard (for AMD) or B760 (for Intel) offers the best balance of features and price for most builds. Don’t pay for a premium Z-series board unless you plan to overclock.

RAM (Memory)

For gaming, 16GB is the minimum. 32GB is the sweet spot for 2025. Stick with DDR5 if your motherboard supports it—it’s faster and future-proof.

Speed matters: Aim for DDR5-6000 CL30 for AMD builds, or DDR5-5600+ for Intel. Higher speeds (like 6400) often cause instability on AMD systems.

Storage (SSD)

Get an NVMe M.2 SSD. Period. A 1TB drive costs around $60–$80 and will make your PC feel lightning-fast. Add a 2TB or 4TB SATA SSD later if you need bulk storage.

Avoid: Hard drives (HDDs) for your operating system. They’re slow, noisy, and ancient. Use them only for backups.

Power Supply (PSU)

The most overlooked component. A cheap PSU can fry your entire system. Use the PSU Tier List as a reference.

  • Wattage: 550W for budget builds, 650W for mid-range, 750W+ for high-end.
  • Rating: 80+ Gold is the sweet spot for efficiency and reliability.

Rule of thumb: Never skimp on the PSU. A $40 unit is a red flag.

Case

Pick a case with good airflow—mesh front panels are best. Avoid glass-front cases that choke your fans. Also check:

  • GPU clearance: Make sure your card fits (length and width).
  • Cable management space: A few inches behind the motherboard tray helps a lot.

My go-to: The Fractal Design Pop Air ($90) is affordable, has great airflow, and looks clean.

Step 3: Gather Your Tools (You Already Have Them)

You don’t need a special toolkit. Just grab:

  • A #2 Phillips-head screwdriver (magnetic tip helps).
  • A clean, flat surface (a wooden desk or table—avoid carpet for static reasons).
  • Your motherboard manual (read it, seriously).
  • Zip ties or velcro straps for cable management.

Optional but nice: An anti-static wrist strap. I’ve built dozens of PCs without one and never had an issue, but if you’re nervous, spend $5 for peace of mind.

Step 4: Assembly – The Order That Works

Follow this sequence. It saves time and frustration.

1. Install the CPU

Open the socket lever, align the triangle marker on the CPU with the triangle on the socket, and drop it in. Do not force it. If it doesn’t sit flat, you’re misaligned. Close the lever gently.

2. Install the RAM

Push the sticks into slots A2 and B2 (check your manual—usually the second and fourth slots from the CPU). You’ll hear a click on both ends. Press evenly.

3. Install the M.2 SSD

Screw out the heatsink (if your motherboard has one), insert the SSD at a 30-degree angle, then press down and secure with the screw. It’s that easy.

4. Install the CPU Cooler

  • Stock coolers (included with most CPUs): Apply the pre-applied thermal paste, align the push-pins, and press down until they click.
  • Aftermarket coolers: Apply a pea-sized dot of thermal paste, mount the bracket, and tighten screws in a cross pattern.

Real mistake: I once installed a cooler without removing the plastic peel on the contact plate. Don’t be me. Check for clear plastic before mounting.

5. Install the Power Supply

Mount the PSU in the case (usually bottom-mounted, fan facing down). Route the cables through the nearest cutouts. Don’t plug anything in yet—just route them.

6. Install the Motherboard

Place the I/O shield (the metal plate with cutouts) into the case first. Then lower the motherboard onto the standoffs. Screw it in with the included screws. Don’t overtighten.

7. Install the GPU

Remove the PCIe slot covers on the back of the case. Align the GPU with the top PCIe x16 slot (the one closest to the CPU). Push down firmly until it clicks. Secure it with screws.

8. Connect All Cables

This is the tedious part. Refer to your motherboard manual for:

  • 24-pin power (biggest cable, goes to motherboard right edge)
  • 8-pin CPU power (usually top-left corner)
  • PCIe power (6+2 pin cables for your GPU)
  • Front panel headers (power button, reset, LEDs—these are tiny and labeled in the manual)

Pro tip: Connect the case fans to the motherboard headers labeled “CHA_FAN” or “SYS_FAN.” If you have RGB fans, you’ll need a separate hub or motherboard RGB header.

Step 5: Cable Management (Do It Right)

You don’t need a perfect build like a YouTuber. But loose cables block airflow and look messy.

  • Route cables behind the motherboard tray. Use the cutouts to bring them back to the front only where needed.
  • Use zip ties to bundle excess cable length.
  • Keep the GPU power cables tidy—they’re the most visible.

One trick: If your case has a shroud (covering the bottom PSU area), hide all extra cables under it.

Step 6: First Boot – The Moment of Truth

Plug in the monitor (to the GPU, not the motherboard), keyboard, and mouse. Flip the PSU switch to “on.” Press the power button.

What should happen:

  • Fans spin.
  • LEDs light up.
  • You see the motherboard logo on screen.

What if nothing happens?

  • Check the PSU switch.
  • Reseat the RAM (remove and reinstall).
  • Make sure the front panel power connector is on the correct pins (consult your manual).

Common issue: The system turns on but no display. This often means the GPU isn’t seated fully, or the monitor is plugged into the motherboard instead of the GPU.

Step 7: Install the Operating System

You’ll need a USB drive (8GB or larger) and another computer to create installation media.

  1. Download the Windows 11 Media Creation Tool from Microsoft’s website (free, no license needed to install).
  2. Run it and select your USB drive.
  3. Plug the USB into your new PC, boot it, and press F12 or DEL repeatedly to enter the boot menu.
  4. Select the USB drive.
  5. Follow the on-screen prompts. When asked for a product key, you can skip it and activate later.

Alternative: If you want to save $100, install Linux (Ubuntu or Pop!_OS). It’s free, lightweight, and works great for web browsing, coding, and light gaming.

Step 8: Driver Installation and Testing

Once Windows is installed, do this immediately:

  1. Update Windows – Settings > Windows Update > Check for updates.
  2. Install GPU drivers – Download from NVIDIA or AMD’s website. Don’t use Windows Update for this.
  3. Motherboard drivers – Download chipset drivers from your motherboard manufacturer’s site (e.g., ASUS, MSI, Gigabyte).
  4. Run a stress test – Use Cinebench (CPU) and FurMark (GPU) for 10 minutes. If temps stay under 85°C, you’re golden.

Real example: After building, my CPU hit 95°C in Cinebench. Turns out I forgot to remove the plastic from the cooler. Fixed it, temps dropped to 72°C. Always check your thermal paste and cooler mount.

Final Thoughts

Building a PC is a skill you can learn in an afternoon. The first build takes 2–4 hours. By your third, you’ll do it in under an hour. You’ll also save hundreds of dollars over prebuilts, and you’ll never be afraid to swap a part again.

If you hit a wall, the r/buildapc subreddit is full of helpful people. Or just Google your specific problem—chances are someone else has solved it.

Now go build something. And flip that PSU switch on first.

item.title: Best Mechanical Keyboards for Programming in 2024
item.description: Ditch the wrist pain. We tested 12 mechanical keyboards for coding. Find your perfect switch, layout, and budget with real-world benchmarks.
item.content:encoded:
TITLE: Best Mechanical Keyboards for Programming in 2024 DESCRIPTION: Ditch the wrist pain. We tested 12 mechanical keyboards for coding. Find your perfect switch, layout, and budget with real-world benchmarks. TAGS: mechanical keyboard, programming keyboard, best keyboard for coders, ergonomic keyboard, Cherry MX switches

Introduction

Let’s be honest: you spend more time touching your keyboard than you do your bed. For a programmer, the keyboard is the primary tool—the interface between your brain and the machine. Yet most devs I know are typing on a flimsy $20 membrane board that came with a pre-built desktop, wondering why their fingers ache after a four-hour debugging session.

I’ve been a full-stack developer for eight years. I’ve written code on everything from a 2012 MacBook butterfly keyboard (a nightmare) to a custom-built split ergonomic board. The difference between a bad keyboard and a great one isn’t just comfort—it’s accuracy, speed, and reduced fatigue over a 10-hour workday.

This isn’t a list of “cool-looking” keyboards. These are the boards I’ve personally tested for at least two weeks of production coding. I’ll cover switch types, layouts, and the specific trade-offs programmers need to consider.

Why Your Keyboard Matters More Than Your Monitor (Almost)

A 1440p monitor is nice. A keyboard that forces you to bottom out keys with 80 grams of force is a repetitive strain injury waiting to happen.

Programmers type differently than gamers or writers. We use modifier keys constantly (Ctrl, Alt, Shift, Cmd, Super). We navigate with arrow keys and Home/End. We hold down Shift while pressing brackets. The wrong keyboard can make if (condition) { feel like a finger-twister.

The three most important factors for a coding keyboard are:

  1. Switch feel – The tactile or linear response that matches your typing style.
  2. Layout efficiency – How easy it is to reach modifiers, arrows, and function keys without moving your hands.
  3. Build quality – Will it survive two years of aggressive :wq spamming?

The Switch Debate: Linear vs. Tactile vs. Clicky

This is the first decision you’ll make, and it’s the most personal. I’ll break down what each feels like for actual coding, not marketing copy.

Linear Switches (e.g., Cherry MX Red, Gateron Yellow)

Linear switches have no tactile bump. You press straight down until the key bottoms out. They’re smooth, quiet, and require less force.

For programmers: Great if you type lightly and prefer a “glassy” feel. They’re excellent for rapid, repeated keystrokes like dd in Vim. The downside? No tactile feedback means you might accidentally press a key halfway and not register it. I used linear switches for a year and found myself missing keystrokes during fast typing.

Tactile Switches (e.g., Cherry MX Brown, Gateron Brown, Topre)

Tactile switches have a small bump halfway through the press. You feel exactly when the key actuates.

For programmers: This is the default recommendation for coding. The bump confirms the keypress without needing to slam the key to the bottom. It reduces fatigue because you don’t have to “bottom out.” I’ve been coding on Gateron Browns for two years—they’re the sweet spot between feedback and noise.

Clicky Switches (e.g., Cherry MX Blue, Kailh Box Jade)

Clicky switches have a tactile bump and an audible click. They’re loud.

For programmers: Only if you have a private office. The click is satisfying for typing prose, but for coding—where you’re constantly hitting Enter, Backspace, and brackets—it gets annoying fast. Your coworkers will hate you. I tested MX Blues for a week and switched back because the noise made me slower.

Actionable tip: Buy a switch tester (a small keychain with 4-6 different switches) before committing to a full board. It costs $10 and saves you from a $150 mistake.

Layout: Full-Size vs. Tenkeyless vs. 60% vs. 75%

Programmers have strong opinions about layout. Here’s the practical difference.

Full-Size (104 keys)

Includes a number pad. If you do data entry or heavy numerical work (spreadsheets, database queries), the numpad is useful. But for pure coding, it pushes your mouse hand too far to the right, causing shoulder strain.

Tenkeyless (TKL, 87 keys)

Removes the numpad. This is the most balanced layout for programmers. Your mouse sits closer to your body, reducing shoulder reach. You still have dedicated arrow keys, Home, End, Page Up, Page Down—essential for navigating code without the mouse.

60% (61 keys)

Removes the function row, arrow keys, and navigation cluster. You access them via layers (e.g., holding Fn + WASD for arrows). This is popular among Vim users who never touch arrows anyway. I used a 60% for six months. It’s great for portability (fits in a backpack), but frustrating for debugging when you need to hit F5 quickly.

75% (84 keys)

A compact layout that keeps the function row and arrows but squeezes them together. It’s the best compromise. I now use a 75% as my daily driver—it has everything I need without wasting desk space.

My recommendation: If you’re new to mechanical keyboards, start with a TKL. You can always downsize later.

The Best Mechanical Keyboards for Programming (Tested)

I tested each of these boards for at least two weeks of actual coding—Python, JavaScript, Go, and shell scripting. Here are the ones that earned a spot on my desk.

1. Keychron V1 (75%, $84)

Best budget option for serious coders.

The Keychron V1 is a 75% layout with hot-swappable switches (you can change switches without soldering). It comes with Gateron Brown switches out of the box—the tactile bump is mild but present. The build is solid: a plastic case with a steel plate, but it doesn’t feel cheap.

Why it’s great for programming: The QMK/VIA firmware support lets you remap every single key. I remapped Caps Lock to Escape (essential for Vim) and set the right modifier keys to match my workflow. The USB-C port is on the left side, which keeps the cable out of the way.

Downside: The stock keycaps are thin ABS plastic—they’ll develop a shine after six months. Budget $20 for a replacement PBT keycap set.

2. Ducky One 3 TKL (TKL, $119)

Best for reliability and out-of-box feel.

Ducky is a Taiwanese brand known for bulletproof build quality. The One 3 TKL uses Cherry MX switches (I tested it with MX Browns). The stabilizers are pre-lubed, so the spacebar and shift keys don’t rattle.

Why it’s great for programming: The keycaps are doubleshot PBT—they’ll never fade or shine. The layout is standard TKL, so your muscle memory works immediately. It has a “dip switch” on the bottom that lets you swap the Caps Lock and Ctrl keys without software.

Downside: No hot-swap capability. If you want to try different switches, you’ll need to desolder. Also, no wireless option.

3. Wooting 60HE (60%, $175)

Best for speed and customization (if you can handle the layout).

The Wooting 60HE uses analog magnetic switches, not mechanical contacts. You can adjust the actuation point from 0.1mm to 4.0mm in software. For programming, this is a game-changer: you can set the actuation point high (like 1.5mm) for light, fast keystrokes without accidental presses.

Why it’s great for programming: The “Rapid Trigger” feature lets you reset the key without fully releasing it—ideal for rapid tapping in Vim or VS Code. The software is excellent and runs on Windows, Mac, and Linux.

Downside: It’s a 60% layout. You need to learn layers for arrows and function keys. Also, the magnetic switches feel different from traditional mechanical switches—some people love it, some hate it.

4. HHKB Professional Classic (60%, $260)

Best for Vim enthusiasts and minimalists.

The Happy Hacking Keyboard (HHKB) is a cult classic among developers. It uses Topre electrostatic capacitive switches—a hybrid between mechanical and membrane that feels like typing on a warm, soft marshmallow. The layout is unique: it moves the Control key to where Caps Lock usually is (perfect for Emacs and Vim) and removes the bottom row modifiers.

Why it’s great for programming: The layout is designed specifically for Unix-based coding. The Control key position alone saves thousands of finger stretches per day. The Topre switches are quiet and have a satisfying “thock” sound.

Downside: The price. Also, no programmability out of the box—you can’t remap keys without buying an external controller. It’s a commitment.

5. ZSA Moonlander (Split, $365)

Best for ergonomics and preventing RSI.

If you’ve ever had wrist pain, this is the endgame keyboard. The Moonlander is a split ortholinear board—the keys are in a grid, not staggered. Each half can be tilted, tented, and rotated independently. You type with your hands shoulder-width apart, which keeps your wrists straight.

Why it’s great for programming: The thumb clusters give you six extra keys per hand. I mapped Backspace, Enter, Tab, and Escape to my thumbs—my pinky fingers haven’t stretched that far in months. The on-board software (Oryx) lets you create complex layers and macros.

Downside: The learning curve is brutal. Expect two weeks of typing at 20 words per minute. Also, it’s expensive.

Actionable Tips for Choosing Your Programming Keyboard

1. Test switches before buying. Go to a local electronics store or buy a switch tester. Switches feel different than they sound in YouTube reviews.

2. Prioritize PBT keycaps. ABS keycaps get shiny and slippery after a few months. PBT keycaps are textured and last years. Most budget boards ship with ABS—factor in a $20-30 upgrade.

3. Ignore “gaming” features. You don’t need RGB lighting, programmable macros for “quick reload,” or a polling rate of 1000Hz. You need accurate, comfortable switches and a layout that doesn’t require hand gymnastics.

4. Consider your OS. Mac users need a keyboard with a dedicated Command key (or software to swap Alt and Win). Windows/Linux users are fine with standard layouts. Some boards (like Keychron) include Mac keycaps in the box.

5. Buy from a vendor with a return policy. Mechanical keyboards are personal. What works for me might not work for you. MechanicalKeyboards.com and Drop both have reasonable return windows.

Conclusion

Your keyboard is the most-used tool in your programming arsenal. A bad one will slow you down and hurt your hands. A good one will become invisible—you’ll forget you’re even typing.

Start with the Keychron V1 if you’re on a budget. Go for the Ducky One 3 if you want something that just works. Splurge on the HHKB or Moonlander if you’ve been coding for years and want to optimize every keystroke.

The best keyboard for programming is the one that makes you want to type. Now go remap your Caps Lock to Escape and get back to writing code.

item.title: Best Smart Home Devices 2025: Top Picks for Real Homes
item.description: Tired of gimmicks? Here are the best smart home devices of 2025 that actually work, save time, and integrate seamlessly. Real reviews, no hype.
item.content:encoded:
TITLE: Best Smart Home Devices 2025: Top Picks for Real Homes DESCRIPTION: Tired of gimmicks? Here are the best smart home devices of 2025 that actually work, save time, and integrate seamlessly. Real reviews, no hype. TAGS: smart home 2025, best smart devices, home automation, smart home tech, 2025 gadgets

Introduction

I’ve been testing smart home gear for over a decade. And I’ll be honest: most years, the “next big thing” is just last year’s gadget with a voice assistant that doesn’t understand your accent. But 2025 feels different. The noise is finally dying down. Instead of promising to “revolutionize your morning routine,” the devices that actually matter are solving specific, annoying problems—like lights that flicker when the microwave runs, or a thermostat that can’t figure out you left the front door open.

This year, the winners aren’t the flashiest. They’re the ones that make your home feel less like a tech demo and more like… a home. I’ve spent the last six months living with, breaking, and sometimes returning dozens of devices. Below are the ones I’d actually recommend to a friend—no affiliate fluff, just what works.

The Smart Home Shifts That Matter in 2025

Before we dive into specific products, a quick reality check. Three trends define this year’s best buys:

Matter is (finally) real. The universal smart home standard launched in 2022 but felt like a committee project. In 2025, most new devices ship with Matter 1.3 support out of the box. That means you can buy a light bulb from brand A, a switch from brand B, and control both with any hub—no proprietary app required. Finally.

Local processing beats cloud dependency. After last year’s major server outages (looking at you, Ring), manufacturers are moving intelligence on-device. The best 2025 devices work even when your internet goes down. Your smart lock should still unlock, your thermostat should still schedule.

Energy awareness is baked in. With variable electricity pricing spreading across the US and EU, the smartest devices now track not just how much energy you use, but when. They’ll delay running your dishwasher until rates drop at 11 PM—without you lifting a finger.

Best Smart Hub: Homey Pro (2025 Edition)

If you only buy one device this year, make it the hub. The Homey Pro has been quietly dominating European smart homes for years, and in 2025 it finally landed in North America with full Matter support. Why does it beat the competition?

Local control, no subscription. Unlike SmartThings (which now charges for advanced automations) or Amazon’s Alexa (which pushes ads), Homey Pro runs everything locally. You connect your devices via Zigbee, Z-Wave, Thread, Wi-Fi, or Matter—and all automations execute on the hub itself. No cloud, no fees, no “Alexa, why did you ignore me?”

Real-world example: I set up an automation that dims the living room lights when I start a movie on my Apple TV. It also tells the robot vacuum to pause, and lowers the smart blinds. Setup took three minutes using Homey’s visual flow editor—no coding. When my internet went down for four hours last month, that automation still ran perfectly.

Actionable tip: If you’re starting from scratch, buy the Homey Pro first. It’s $399, but it replaces three separate hubs you’d otherwise need. Over two years, you’ll save money and sanity.

Best Smart Thermostat: Ecobee Premium (2025 Firmware Update)

Nest dominates the conversation, but Ecobee has quietly become the smarter choice. The 2025 firmware update added something Nest still lacks: room-by-room occupancy detection using radar.

Here’s how it works: Instead of guessing whether you’re home based on your phone’s location (which drains battery), the Ecobee uses low-power radar sensors to detect if someone is actually in the living room. If you’re watching TV in the den, it stops heating the bedrooms. It also learns your home’s thermal lag—how long it takes for rooms to warm up after the furnace kicks on.

Real-world savings: My December gas bill dropped 18% compared to last year, despite similar weather. The thermostat also now integrates with local utility demand-response programs. During peak grid strain, it pre-cools my house before 4 PM, then lets it drift up gradually—so I never notice, but the grid does.

What to watch for: Ecobee still uses a proprietary sensor for remote rooms. Buy the 3-pack sensor bundle ($79) on day one. Without them, the “room-by-room” feature is limited.

Best Smart Lighting: Philips Hue with Matter + Dynamic Scenes

Philips Hue has been the gold standard for years, but in 2025, the system finally got a meaningful upgrade: dynamic scenes that shift color temperature throughout the day.

This isn’t just “set a warm light at night.” The new firmware uses your local sunrise/sunset times to gradually shift from cool blue morning light to warm amber evening tones. It mimics natural daylight patterns, and it actually helps with sleep. I’ve been using it for three months, and my sleep tracker shows I’m falling asleep 22 minutes faster on average.

Why not cheaper alternatives? I tested WiZ, Govee, and IKEA’s smart lights. They’re fine for color parties, but their color accuracy at low brightness is poor—whites look pinkish below 10%. Hue stays neutral. And with Matter support, you don’t need the Hue Bridge anymore (though it’s still recommended for complex automations).

Actionable tip: Start with one Hue Gradient Lightstrip behind your TV. It syncs with on-screen content for movies, but also works as a bias light that reduces eye strain. Cost: $89. Worth every penny.

Best Smart Lock: Level Lock+ with Matter

Smart locks have a reputation for being bulky, ugly, and battery-draining. The Level Lock+ solves all three. It fits inside your existing deadbolt—so from the outside, it looks like a normal lock. No keypad, no fingerprint reader, no bulky exterior plate.

How it works: You unlock it with your phone (via Thread, which is faster and more reliable than Bluetooth), Apple Watch, or a physical key. The 2025 model adds a built-in Thread radio that connects directly to your Homey or Apple Home hub—no bridge needed. Battery life is rated at one year, but I’m at nine months and still at 70%.

Real-world test: I handed a house-sitter a temporary digital key that only worked between 3 PM and 8 PM, and only for the front door. It revoked automatically. No physical key to copy, no code to change. That’s the killer feature.

What it lacks: No built-in keypad. If you want keyless entry for kids or guests, you’ll need the separate Level Keypad ($69). It’s a minor hassle, but the trade-off for the lock’s discreet design is worth it.

Best Robot Vacuum: Roborock Q Revo MaxV

Robot vacuums are finally useful. The 2025 Roborock Q Revo MaxV is the first I’ve tested that genuinely doesn’t need human intervention for weeks.

Key upgrades over 2024 models:

  • Self-emptying base that holds 60 days of dust.
  • Self-washing mop pads that scrub themselves clean after every room. No more pushing a damp, smelly cloth across your floors.
  • Obstacle avoidance that actually works. It recognizes cables, socks, and even pet waste (yes, it avoids it). My old Roomba ate a charging cable. This one sees it and goes around.

Real-world use: I set it to run nightly at 2 AM. It vacuums the whole house, mops the kitchen and bathrooms, then returns to the base to empty and wash. I empty the dust bag once every two months. That’s it.

Price: $999. It’s expensive, but if you have hard floors and pets, it saves hours per week. The cheaper Roborock Q5 ($599) is fine for vacuum-only homes.

Best Smart Smoke Detector: Google Nest Protect (Still)

This is the only device on this list that hasn’t been redesigned in years. And that’s fine. The Nest Protect (launched in 2013, last updated in 2020) remains the best smart smoke and CO detector because it does one thing perfectly: it tells you where the danger is, and what to do about it.

When smoke from burnt toast triggers it, it says “Heads-up, smoke detected in the kitchen” in a calm voice—not a deafening alarm. If it’s real smoke, it escalates to the full 85dB siren. It also sends push notifications to your phone, so you know if your vacation home’s alarm is going off.

Why no 2025 upgrade needed: The hardware is mature. The sensors are reliable. The app works. Don’t fix what isn’t broken. Buy the wired version ($119) for best reliability.

Warning: Do not buy the cheaper First Alert Onelink. I tested it. False alarms every two weeks. Returned it.

Actionable Tips for Building Your 2025 Smart Home

  1. Start with the hub. Don’t buy devices first and hope they work together. Buy the Homey Pro or Apple Home hub, then add devices that support Matter.
  2. Prioritize wired over battery. Hardwired devices (thermostats, smoke detectors, smart switches) are more reliable. Reserve battery for locks and sensors.
  3. Skip voice assistants as the primary interface. Voice is great for “turn off the lights,” but terrible for complex automations. Use the hub’s app or physical buttons.
  4. Check your Wi-Fi. Smart home devices hate mesh networks with weak backhaul. If you have a mesh system, wire the nodes via Ethernet if possible. Or buy a dedicated Thread network (most 2025 hubs include it).
  5. Buy one device at a time. Install it, live with it for a week, then add the next. Smart home burnout is real—and expensive.

Final Thoughts

The best smart home in 2025 isn’t the one with the most gadgets. It’s the one that gets out of your way. The devices above do that. They work when the internet is down, they don’t require a monthly subscription, and they solve actual problems—not invented ones.

If I had to pick just three: the Homey Pro hub, an Ecobee thermostat, and a Roborock vacuum. That’s 80% of the value for 40% of the cost. Everything else is icing.

Now go turn off that light with your phone. You’ve earned it.

item.title: WiFi 6 vs WiFi 6E: Key Differences Explained
item.description: WiFi 6 vs WiFi 6E: What’s the real difference? Learn about the 6 GHz band, device compatibility, speed gains, and whether upgrading is worth it in 2024.
item.content:encoded:
TITLE: WiFi 6 vs WiFi 6E: Key Differences Explained DESCRIPTION: WiFi 6 vs WiFi 6E: What’s the real difference? Learn about the 6 GHz band, device compatibility, speed gains, and whether upgrading is worth it in 2024. TAGS: WiFi 6, WiFi 6E, 6 GHz band, wireless networking, router upgrade, tech comparison

Introduction

You just bought a shiny new WiFi 6 router, and suddenly your tech-obsessed friend tells you, “Should have waited for WiFi 6E.” Now you’re wondering if you made a mistake. Or maybe you’re still on that ISP-provided router from 2017, and the alphabet soup of “6” and “6E” feels like a marketing gimmick designed to sell you something you don’t need.

Here’s the truth: WiFi 6E is not a faster version of WiFi 6. It’s a different version. Think of it like a highway. WiFi 6 widened the lanes on the existing road. WiFi 6E built an entirely new, private express lane with almost no traffic. The difference matters—but only if you know what you’re looking at.

Let’s cut through the jargon. I’ll walk you through what changed, why the 6 GHz band is a big deal, and—most importantly—whether you should spend your money on a WiFi 6E router today or stick with WiFi 6 for another year.

What is WiFi 6? (A Quick Refresher)

Before we dig into the “E,” let’s make sure we’re on the same page about WiFi 6. Officially called 802.11ax, WiFi 6 was introduced in 2019 as the successor to WiFi 5 (802.11ac). It wasn’t just about raw speed—it was about efficiency.

Key improvements in WiFi 6:

  • OFDMA (Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiple Access): Think of this as a delivery truck that can carry packages for multiple houses at once, instead of making separate trips for each. It reduces latency and improves performance in crowded homes with lots of devices.
  • MU-MIMO (Multi-User, Multiple Input, Multiple Output): WiFi 6 improved MU-MIMO to handle uplink and downlink traffic simultaneously. Your router can now talk to multiple devices at the same time, not just one after another.
  • 1024-QAM: A denser modulation scheme that packs 25% more data into each signal compared to WiFi 5’s 256-QAM.
  • Target Wake Time (TWT): A battery-saving feature where your router and device agree on a “nap schedule.” Your phone can sleep longer between data bursts, extending battery life.

WiFi 6 operates on the same two frequency bands we’ve used for years: 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz. It’s backward compatible, so your old iPhone 8 will connect to a WiFi 6 router just fine—it just won’t get the new features.

What is WiFi 6E? The 6 GHz Game Changer

WiFi 6E is exactly the same technology as WiFi 6—same OFDMA, same MU-MIMO, same 1024-QAM. The “E” stands for Extended. What makes it different is the 6 GHz band.

For the first time in WiFi history, regulators (including the FCC in the U.S.) opened up a massive chunk of unlicensed spectrum in the 6 GHz range: 1,200 MHz of additional airwaves. To put that in perspective, the entire 5 GHz band is only about 500 MHz wide. The 2.4 GHz band is just 80 MHz.

This matters because:

  • Less congestion: Very few devices currently use 6 GHz. Your neighbor’s baby monitor, your microwave, and the Bluetooth speaker aren’t there. It’s like having a party where only your invited guests show up.
  • Wider channels: WiFi 6E supports 160 MHz-wide channels natively. In 5 GHz, those wide channels are often blocked by radar or DFS (Dynamic Frequency Selection) restrictions. In 6 GHz, you get the full width, which translates to higher throughput per device.
  • Lower latency: With no interference from legacy devices, latency drops. For real-time applications like video calls, cloud gaming, or VR headsets, this is a tangible improvement.

Real-world example: I tested a WiFi 6E router in a dense apartment building. On WiFi 6 (5 GHz), my laptop showed 520 Mbps with a ping of 14 ms. Switching to the 6 GHz band on the same router, the same laptop hit 780 Mbps with a ping of 4 ms. The router didn’t change—the airspace did.

Speed and Performance: What the Numbers Actually Mean

Let’s do a quick spec comparison without the marketing fluff.

Feature WiFi 6 (2.4/5 GHz) WiFi 6E (adds 6 GHz)
Max theoretical speed 9.6 Gbps 9.6 Gbps
Available spectrum ~600 MHz +1,200 MHz
Typical real-world speed 400–800 Mbps 600–1,200 Mbps
Latency (local network) 5–15 ms 2–5 ms
Channel width support Up to 160 MHz (often limited) Full 160 MHz, no restrictions

Notice that the theoretical maximum is the same. WiFi 6E doesn’t magically make data travel faster. But in practice, because you’re not sharing the air with dozens of other devices, your actual throughput is higher and more consistent.

Actionable tip: If you’re a gamer, the lower latency on 6 GHz is the biggest selling point. For a Netflix streamer, you likely won’t notice the difference between 500 Mbps and 800 Mbps—your internet plan is probably the bottleneck anyway.

Device Compatibility: The Biggest Catch

Here’s where the reality check hits. WiFi 6E requires new hardware on both ends—the router and the client device (phone, laptop, tablet). There is no backward compatibility with 6 GHz.

  • WiFi 6 devices (like an iPhone 11, Samsung Galaxy S10) will connect to a WiFi 6E router, but only on the 2.4 or 5 GHz bands. They cannot see the 6 GHz network.
  • WiFi 6E devices include the iPhone 15 Pro, Samsung Galaxy S23 Ultra, Google Pixel 8, and laptops with Intel AX210 or newer chipsets. If your device was released before late 2022, it almost certainly does not support 6 GHz.
  • WiFi 5 or older devices will work on a WiFi 6E router, but again, only on 2.4 or 5 GHz.

The trap: Buying a WiFi 6E router today means you’re paying a premium for a feature that maybe two of your devices can use. If you live alone and own a WiFi 6E laptop, great. If you have a family with a mix of iPhones, iPads, and smart home gadgets, most of them will never touch the 6 GHz band.

Practical advice: Check your device list. Go to Settings > About Phone or System Information on your laptop. Look for “WiFi 6E” or “802.11ax 6 GHz” in the wireless specs. If you don’t see it, you’re not getting the benefit.

Range and Obstacles: The Trade-Off

Higher frequency radio waves have a physical downside: they don’t travel as far, and they struggle more with walls and floors. 6 GHz is even higher than 5 GHz, so its range is shorter.

  • 2.4 GHz: Best range, penetrates walls and floors well. Max speed, but crowded.
  • 5 GHz: Good range, decent wall penetration. Balanced for most homes.
  • 6 GHz: Shortest range. One or two walls can drop the signal significantly. Best used in the same room as the router.

Real example: In my two-story house, the WiFi 6E signal from the living room router reached the upstairs bedroom at about 60% strength. The 5 GHz signal was at 85%. The 2.4 GHz signal was at 95%. If your router is in a closet in the basement, 6 GHz is practically useless on the second floor.

Actionable tip: If you buy a WiFi 6E router, place it in a central, open location. Avoid putting it behind a TV, inside a cabinet, or near metal objects. For whole-home coverage, you’ll likely need a mesh system that includes 6 GHz backhaul—but that gets expensive fast.

Use Cases: Who Actually Benefits?

Not everyone needs WiFi 6E. Here’s a quick self-assessment:

You should consider WiFi 6E if:

  • You use VR headsets (Meta Quest 3, Apple Vision Pro) and want wireless PC streaming with minimal lag.
  • You’re a competitive gamer who plays latency-sensitive titles (Valorant, CS2, fighting games) over WiFi.
  • You live in a densely populated area (apartment building, condo) where 5 GHz is congested with neighbor networks.
  • You frequently transfer large files (video editing, 4K/8K footage) between devices on your local network.

You’re fine with WiFi 6 if:

  • Your internet plan is under 500 Mbps. Your ISP is the bottleneck, not your WiFi.
  • You mostly stream video, browse the web, and do video calls. WiFi 6 handles these perfectly.
  • You have a mix of older devices (laptops from 2020, iPhones from 2019, smart plugs, etc.). They won’t use 6 GHz anyway.
  • You’re on a budget. WiFi 6 routers are now affordable (under $100), while WiFi 6E routers start around $200 and go up.

Price and Availability: The Upgrade Timeline

WiFi 6 routers have been on the market since 2019. By 2024, they’re mature, stable, and cheap. You can get a decent WiFi 6 router (like the TP-Link Archer AX55) for around $80. A high-end WiFi 6E router (like the Asus ROG Rapture GT-AXE11000) costs $350–$400.

WiFi 6E is still in its early adopter phase. Prices are dropping, but not quickly. The sweet spot is likely late 2024 to early 2025, when WiFi 7 starts rolling out and pushes 6E prices down.

My recommendation: If you’re building a new network from scratch and have a WiFi 6E-capable device, go ahead and buy a 6E router. The extra $100–$150 gives you future-proofing and immediate benefits for that one device. But if you’re upgrading an existing WiFi 5 network, a good WiFi 6 router is the smarter, more cost-effective choice today.

The Bottom Line: Which One Should You Buy?

WiFi 6 and WiFi 6E are not competitors. WiFi 6E is an add-on to WiFi 6. It’s the same technology, running on cleaner, less crowded airwaves.

  • Buy WiFi 6 if you want reliable, fast, affordable wireless for a household with multiple devices. It’s the best value in 2024.
  • Buy WiFi 6E if you have specific high-bandwidth, low-latency needs (VR, gaming, large file transfers) and own at least one device that supports the 6 GHz band.

Don’t let marketing convince you that WiFi 6E is a revolution. It’s an evolution—a meaningful one for certain users, but not a must-have for everyone. The real game changer will be WiFi 7, which promises multi-link operation and speeds over 30 Gbps. But that’s a story for another post.

For now, check your devices, check your internet speed, and make the call that fits your actual usage. Your wallet—and your WiFi—will thank you.

item.title: Best Budget Drones 2025: Top Picks Under $500
item.description: The best budget drones of 2025 tested for real-world use. From 4K cameras to GPS stability, find the perfect drone without breaking the bank.
item.content:encoded:
TITLE: Best Budget Drones 2025: Top Picks Under $500 DESCRIPTION: The best budget drones of 2025 tested for real-world use. From 4K cameras to GPS stability, find the perfect drone without breaking the bank. TAGS: budget drones, cheap drones 2025, best drones under 500, beginner drones, drone reviews

Introduction

I’ll be honest: two years ago, I thought a “budget drone” meant a plastic toy that would fly into a tree within 30 seconds. And for a long time, that was true. But 2025 is different. The technology that used to cost $1,000 has trickled down into sub-$500 models. We are talking obstacle avoidance, 4K HDR video, GPS return-to-home, and battery life that actually lets you film more than one clip before running out.

I’ve personally flown over a dozen drones in the past three months to write this guide. I crashed one (RIP, little guy), lost another to a gust of wind, and returned two that simply weren’t worth the plastic they were made of. Below are the ones that survived my testing and actually earn a spot in your gear bag.

What Changed in 2025 for Budget Drones?

The biggest shift this year is the arrival of reliable sub-$300 GPS drones. In 2023, GPS on a cheap drone was a gimmick—it locked satellites slowly and drifted like a shopping cart with a broken wheel. In 2025, companies like Potensic and Holy Stone have licensed better chipset modules. The result? Budget drones that hover in place during a 15 mph breeze.

Also, the camera war has moved. Everyone talks about “4K,” but the real upgrade is image stabilization. Mechanical gimbals used to be reserved for $800+ drones. Now, you can get a 3-axis mechanical gimbal on a $350 drone. That is the difference between a video that looks like a home movie and one that looks like a travel vlog.

The Top 5 Budget Drones of 2025

I’ve categorized these by use case, not just price. Because the “best” drone for a hiker is different from the “best” drone for a teenager’s first flight.

1. DJI Mini 4K (2025 Edition) – Best Overall Under $300

Price: $299 Why it wins: DJI finally dropped the price on their entry-level model while keeping the good stuff.

The DJI Mini 4K is not a new drone—it’s a repackaged Mini 2 SE with a better sensor. But that is exactly what the market needed. It shoots 4K at 30fps with a 1/2.3-inch CMOS sensor. The 3-axis gimbal is rock solid. In my test flight over a lake, the footage was stable enough to use in an edit without any post-stabilization.

Real-world performance:

  • Flight time: 31 minutes (I got 28 in windy conditions)
  • Range: 10 km (OcuSync 2.0 still works like magic)
  • Weight: Under 249 grams (no FAA registration in the US)

The catch: No obstacle avoidance. You must fly carefully. Also, the camera struggles in low light. If you only fly during golden hour, the Mini 4K is fine. If you want to shoot at dusk, look at the next option.

Actionable tip: Buy the “Fly More Combo” for $50 extra. Three batteries mean you can fly for nearly an hour. The single battery is a tease.

2. Potensic ATOM SE – Best Value for Hikers

Price: $269 Why it wins: It folds smaller than a water bottle and has a mechanical gimbal at this price.

The Potensic ATOM SE surprised me. I took it on a 5-mile hike in the Rockies. At 248 grams, it fits in a side pocket of a hiking pack. The Sony CMOS sensor captures surprisingly detailed 4K footage. But the real win is the PixSync 2.0 transmission system. It held connection at over 2 miles in an open field. That is DJI-level performance for half the price.

Real-world performance:

  • Flight time: 30 minutes per battery
  • Wind resistance: Level 5 (handled 20 mph gusts)
  • Gimbal: 3-axis mechanical

The catch: The app is clunky. It takes about 30 seconds to connect on startup. Also, the controller feels a bit cheap in the hands—plastic-y, like a toy. But the drone itself flies like a premium product.

Actionable tip: Calibrate the compass every time you change locations. If you hike from a valley to a ridge, the magnetic field changes enough to cause drift. A 10-second calibration fixes it.

3. Holy Stone HS720G – Best for Beginners Who Want GPS

Price: $199 Why it wins: It is the most forgiving drone on this list.

The Holy Stone HS720G is not the sharpest camera drone. But if you have never flown before, this is the one to buy. It has GPS-assisted hover that locks position within 5 seconds of takeoff. The optical flow sensor keeps it stable even when GPS signal is weak (under trees or near buildings).

Real-world performance:

  • Flight time: 26 minutes (realistic: 20)
  • Camera: 4K (but softer than DJI/Potensic)
  • Features: Return-to-home, follow-me mode, orbit mode

The catch: The “4K” camera is upscaled from 2.7K. You cannot pixel-peep on a computer monitor. But for social media posts (Instagram, TikTok), it looks fine. Also, the drone is heavier (450 grams), so you need to register it with the FAA.

Actionable tip: Use the “Follow Me” mode when biking. It tracks GPS from the controller, not visual recognition, so it works even if you wear the same color as the background. Just set the altitude to 10 meters to avoid trees.

4. Ruko F11 Pro 2 – Best Battery Life Under $500

Price: $349 Why it wins: 60 minutes of total flight time (two batteries included).

Battery anxiety is real. The Ruko F11 Pro 2 solves it by giving you two batteries in the box. Each battery lasts 30 minutes (I tested 28 in moderate wind). That is enough to film a full property walkthrough or a 2-mile coastline without stopping.

Real-world performance:

  • Camera: 4K with EIS (electronic image stabilization)
  • Range: 1.5 km (solid, not spectacular)
  • Build: Sturdy, crash-resistant landing gear

The catch: Electronic stabilization means you lose about 10% of the frame to cropping. The footage is smooth, but the field of view is narrower than the DJI Mini 4K. Also, the controller screen is bright but not sunlight-readable.

Actionable tip: Use this drone for real estate or construction site inspection. The long battery life means you can fly a full property without rushing. The EIS handles the slight wobble from wind.

5. Autel Robotics EVO Nano+ (Price Drop) – Best Camera Under $500

Price: $499 (down from $799) Why it wins: This is a professional camera on a budget frame.

The Autel EVO Nano+ originally launched at $799. In 2025, it dropped to $499 to compete with DJI. The camera is 50MP stills with a 1/1.28-inch sensor (larger than the DJI Mini 4K). The low-light performance is genuinely impressive. I shot a sunset over a city skyline, and the noise was minimal even at ISO 800.

Real-world performance:

  • Flight time: 28 minutes
  • Obstacle avoidance: 3-way (forward, backward, downward)
  • Video: 4K HDR at 30fps

The catch: The app is less polished than DJI’s. Some users report connection drops at max range. Also, the drone is 249 grams, but the battery is proprietary and expensive ($79 for a spare).

Actionable tip: Use the “Dynamic Track” mode for moving subjects. It locks onto a person or car and follows without needing GPS. This is better than “Follow Me” because it uses visual recognition, so it works indoors.

How to Choose a Budget Drone in 2025

Do not buy based on megapixels alone. Here is a quick decision tree:

  • If you want the best video quality: Get the Autel EVO Nano+ ($499) or DJI Mini 4K ($299). Mechanical gimbal is non-negotiable.
  • If you are a total beginner: Get the Holy Stone HS720G ($199). It is forgiving and cheap to repair.
  • If you need long flight time: Get the Ruko F11 Pro 2 ($349). Two batteries in the box.
  • If you travel/hike: Get the Potensic ATOM SE ($269). It folds tiny and has a mechanical gimbal.

Three Mistakes to Avoid

1. Buying a drone without GPS. If the product page does not say “GPS” or “GLONASS,” do not buy it. Non-GPS drones drift with the wind. You will spend all your time fighting the controls instead of filming.

2. Ignoring the controller. A good drone with a bad controller is a bad experience. Look for controllers with telemetry screens or at least a phone holder that does not wobble. The Holy Stone and Potensic controllers are fine. The Ruko controller is acceptable.

3. Forgetting about spare parts. DJI and Autel sell replacement propellers, arms, and batteries on Amazon. Holy Stone and Ruko do too, but shipping can take two weeks. Before you buy, search for " [drone model] replacement parts " and check if they are in stock.

Final Verdict

The best budget drone in 2025 is the DJI Mini 4K if you want reliability and video quality. It is boring to recommend the market leader, but DJI earned it. The Mini 4K does everything right: stable flight, good range, excellent gimbal.

However, if you want to save $30 and get a slightly better battery setup, the Potensic ATOM SE is a close second. It flies just as well, and the Sony sensor is a nice bonus.

Avoid the no-name brands on Amazon with 10,000 reviews that all say “5 stars, great gift.” Those are usually paid reviews. Stick to the five models above, and you will have a drone that actually flies, films, and returns home.

Now go fly. Just avoid the trees.

item.title: 15 iPhone Tips and Tricks You Probably Didn’t Know
item.description: Unlock hidden iPhone features with these 15 actionable tips. From faster texting to pro-level camera tricks, save time and boost productivity today.
item.content:encoded:
TITLE: 15 iPhone Tips and Tricks You Probably Didn’t Know DESCRIPTION: Unlock hidden iPhone features with these 15 actionable tips. From faster texting to pro-level camera tricks, save time and boost productivity today. TAGS: iPhone tips, iOS shortcuts, iPhone hidden features, tech productivity, Apple tricks

Introduction

Let’s be honest: most of us use maybe 20% of what the iPhone can actually do. The other 80% is buried in menus, hidden behind long presses, or simply never advertised. I’ve been using iPhones since the 3GS, and I still stumble on features that make me wonder how I lived without them.

Last week, a friend watched me scan a document with the Notes app in about four seconds. She thought I was using a third-party scanner. She wasn’t. That’s the kind of gap I want to close for you.

These aren’t the “turn on dark mode” tips you’ve seen a hundred times. These are real, time-saving, battery-extending, workflow-changing tricks that work on iOS 17 and 18. Grab your iPhone and follow along.

Master the Back Tap for Instant Actions

The back of your iPhone is a button you’ve never pressed. It’s called Back Tap, and it’s been hiding in Accessibility settings since iOS 14.

Go to Settings > Accessibility > Touch > Back Tap. You’ll see two options: Double Tap and Triple Tap. Assign an action to each. I use Double Tap to open the Control Center and Triple Tap to take a screenshot. But you can assign almost anything: open an app, mute your phone, launch the flashlight, or trigger a Shortcut.

Real example: I set Triple Tap to open the Magnifier app. When I’m reading tiny restaurant menus in dim light, two quick knocks on the back of the phone and I have a zoomed, brightened view. No fumbling for buttons.

The catch? It works best with a case that doesn’t dampen the tap sensitivity. Thin silicone or plastic cases are fine; thick OtterBox-style cases might require a firmer knock.

The Hidden Trackpad on Your Keyboard

You’ve probably tried to move the cursor by poking at the text. It’s imprecise and frustrating. Here’s the fix: press and hold the space bar until the keyboard turns blank and gray. Now slide your finger anywhere on the keyboard area—the cursor moves exactly where you guide it.

This works in any text field: Messages, Notes, Mail, Safari. Once you get used to it, you’ll never go back to the old way.

Pro tip: If you have a 3D Touch-capable iPhone (iPhone 6s through XS), you can also force-press anywhere on the keyboard to activate this. On newer models without 3D Touch, only the space bar works. On iPads, you can use two fingers on the keyboard to slide the cursor.

Scan Documents Instantly with the Notes App

Don’t download a separate scanning app. The Notes app has a built-in scanner that’s faster and cleaner than most dedicated tools.

Open a new note, tap the camera icon, and select Scan Documents. Hold your phone over the document—it auto-detects the edges and captures the image. You can adjust corners afterward, apply filters (Color, Grayscale, Black & White, Photo), and save as a PDF.

Why this matters: I used to use Adobe Scan. It’s good, but it takes longer to open, syncs to a cloud I don’t always want, and shows ads. The Notes scanner is instant, offline, and stores the PDF directly in the note. You can share it via AirDrop, Mail, or any messaging app right from there.

Use the Hidden Magnifier as a Reading Aid

Your iPhone has a built-in magnifying glass that’s much more than a zoom. It’s actually a full-on digital loupe with contrast, brightness, and color filters.

Find it by triple-clicking the side button (or home button on older models). If it doesn’t open, go to Settings > Accessibility > Magnifier and toggle it on. Once active, you can:

  • Adjust zoom level with a slider
  • Change brightness and contrast
  • Apply color filters (useful for color blindness or low-light reading)
  • Freeze the frame (tap the shutter button) so you can read a tiny label without holding your phone steady

I use this constantly for reading serial numbers on electronics, ingredients on food packaging, and fine print on contracts. It’s also a lifesaver for older family members who refuse to carry reading glasses.

Create Custom Vibration Patterns for Contacts

You can assign a unique vibration pattern to each contact. This way, you know who’s calling without looking at the screen.

Go to Contacts > Select a person > Ringtone > Vibration > Create New Vibration. Tap out a rhythm on the screen—short taps, long presses, pauses—and save it.

Practical use: I gave my wife a pattern of two short taps and a long one. When my phone buzzes in my pocket during a meeting, I know it’s her without pulling it out. I gave my boss a single short tap (so I know I can ignore it if I’m busy). My mom gets a frantic staccato pattern because, well, she’s my mom.

You can do the same for text tones under Sounds & Haptics.

The Secret to One-Handed Keyboard Typing

If you’re using a Pro Max or Plus model, reaching the opposite side of the keyboard with one hand is a stretch. Apple built a one-handed keyboard mode years ago, and almost no one uses it.

Long-press the emoji or globe icon on the keyboard (bottom left). You’ll see three options: left-aligned, centered, and right-aligned keyboard. Tap the left or right alignment depending on which hand you’re using. The keyboard shrinks and shifts to that side.

To go back, tap the empty space on the opposite side of the keyboard.

Why you’ll love this: I type with one hand while holding a coffee cup or carrying groceries. The shifted keyboard puts the most common keys right under my thumb. It’s not perfect for fast typing, but it’s way better than stretching or dropping your phone.

Batch Delete Photos Like a Pro

Deleting photos one by one is painful. The Photos app has a batch selection trick that speeds this up.

Open your photo library, tap Select (top right), then drag your finger across the photos you want to delete. You don’t have to tap each one. Just swipe in a row. For multiple rows, keep your finger down and zigzag.

Advanced trick: To select non-adjacent photos, start dragging to select the first batch, then use a second finger to tap individual photos outside the selection range. This works on iPad too.

Once selected, tap the trash icon. Don’t forget to go to Recently Deleted and permanently clear them if you need the storage back immediately.

Use Siri Shortcuts for Repetitive Tasks

Siri Shortcuts are powerful, but most people ignore them because they seem complicated. Let me simplify: think of a task you do every day that takes three or more steps. That’s a candidate for a Shortcut.

Example: Every morning, I check the weather, turn on my smart lights, and start a 10-minute meditation timer. That’s three separate apps. I created one Shortcut called “Morning Mode” that does all three in sequence. I trigger it by saying, “Hey Siri, Morning Mode.”

To create one:

  1. Open the Shortcuts app (it’s pre-installed, don’t delete it).
  2. Tap the + icon.
  3. Tap Add Action and search for the first app or action (e.g., Weather > Get Current Weather).
  4. Tap the + again to add the next action.
  5. Continue until your sequence is complete.
  6. Name the Shortcut and tap Done.

You can also add Shortcuts to your Home Screen as a button. I have one for “Driving to Work” that opens Apple Maps, starts a podcast, and sends my ETA to my wife. It saves me about 45 seconds every morning.

The Calculator Backspace Swipe

If you type a wrong digit in the Calculator app, don’t tap C and start over. Swipe left or right on the number display. Each swipe deletes the last digit you entered.

This is one of those small features that feels obvious once you know it, but it’s completely invisible. I’ve watched people frantically tap C and re-enter long numbers. One swipe saves the day.

Bonus: Turn your phone sideways to reveal the scientific calculator. It includes logarithms, exponents, and trigonometric functions.

Instantly Share Wi-Fi Passwords Without Typing

You’re at a friend’s house, and they ask for the Wi-Fi password. Instead of reading a long, case-sensitive string, use Apple’s built-in password sharing.

Make sure both devices have Bluetooth and Wi-Fi turned on. The person trying to connect selects your network. You get a pop-up on your phone that says “Share Wi-Fi Password.” Tap Share Password. Done.

Requirements: Both devices must be Apple (iPhone, iPad, or Mac). Both must have each other in their Contacts. If you’re not in their Contacts, it won’t work. In that case, just add each other quickly, or use the old-fashioned method.

This works in reverse too. If you’re the guest, just ask the host to tap their phone when you try to connect.

Use AirDrop with Everyone for 10 Minutes

AirDrop is great, but the default setting (Contacts Only) means you can’t receive files from strangers. If you’re at a conference, party, or family gathering, you can temporarily open AirDrop to everyone.

Go to Control Center > long-press the network card (top left with Wi-Fi/Bluetooth) > tap AirDrop > select Everyone for 10 Minutes. This option was added in iOS 17. It automatically reverts to Contacts Only after 10 minutes, so you don’t accidentally leave it open.

Why this matters: I used to hand my phone to someone so they could AirDrop me a photo. That’s risky. Now they just tap my name from their phone. It’s faster and safer.

The Best Camera Trick: Lock Exposure and Focus

You probably know you can tap to focus. But did you know you can lock both focus and exposure?

Open the Camera app, frame your shot, then tap and hold the subject on the screen until you see “AE/AF Lock” at the top. Now, even if you move the phone or the subject moves slightly, the focus and exposure stay fixed.

Real scenario: You’re filming a cooking video. You want the pan in focus, but your hand moves in and out of frame. Without AE/AF Lock, the camera keeps refocusing on your hand. With it locked, the pan stays sharp and the exposure stays consistent.

To unlock, tap anywhere on the screen.

Use VoiceOver to Read Text Aloud

This one is technically an accessibility feature, but it’s useful for everyone. You can make your iPhone read any text on the screen aloud.

Go to Settings > Accessibility > Spoken Content > Speak Screen. Enable it. Now, swipe down with two fingers from the top of any screen, and Siri will start reading the text. A control panel appears where you can adjust speed, pause, or skip forward.

Use cases: Listen to a long article while driving (pull over first), have a recipe read to you while your hands are dirty, or proofread your own writing by hearing it spoken back. I use this to catch awkward phrasing in emails.

Find Your AirPods with Precision Finding

If you lose an AirPod in the couch cushions, the regular Find My app shows you a map. That’s not helpful when it’s three feet away. If you have AirPods Pro (2nd generation) or AirPods Max, you can use Precision Finding.

Open the Find My app, select your AirPods, and tap Find Nearby. Your iPhone will guide you with an arrow, distance indicator, and haptic feedback. It uses the same U1 chip that helps you find your keys with an AirTag.

Note: This only works with AirPods that have the U1 chip. Older AirPods just show a map. If you’re in the market for new ones, the Pro 2nd gen is worth it for this feature alone.

The Ultimate Battery Health Shortcut

You don’t need to dig into Settings to check battery health. Create a simple Shortcut that shows your battery percentage and health in one tap.

Open Shortcuts, create a new one, and add the action Get Battery Level. Then add Get Device Details and set it to Battery Health. Finally, add Show Result. Name it “Battery Check.” Add it to your Home Screen.

Now, one tap shows you both numbers. I check mine every two weeks to see if I need a battery replacement before it drops below 80%.

Conclusion

The iPhone is a tool that rewards curiosity. Every one of these tips took me less than five minutes to set up, but they’ve saved me hours over the years. The back tap alone probably saves me five seconds every time I need a screenshot—and I take a lot of screenshots.

Start with one or two that solve a real pain point. For me, it was the cursor control and the document scanner. For you, it might be the custom vibrations or the Wi-Fi sharing. Whatever you pick, the goal is the same: make your phone work for you, not the other way around.

Got a tip I missed? I’m always looking for new ones. Try these out, and let me know which one becomes your daily habit.

item.title: How to Set Up a Home NAS Server: A Practical Guide
item.description: Build your own home NAS from scratch. Step-by-step guide covering hardware, software, RAID, and remote access for backups and media streaming.
item.content:encoded:
TITLE: How to Set Up a Home NAS Server: A Practical Guide DESCRIPTION: Build your own home NAS from scratch. Step-by-step guide covering hardware, software, RAID, and remote access for backups and media streaming. TAGS: home NAS, DIY NAS server, network attached storage, home server setup, data backup

Introduction

Last year, I lost three years of family photos when a laptop hard drive failed. The backup drive I’d been using was sitting right next to the laptop on the same desk during a power surge. Both died. That’s when I stopped treating backup as an afterthought and started building a home NAS.

A Network Attached Storage (NAS) is essentially your own private cloud. Unlike Dropbox or Google Drive, you own the hardware, you control the data, and there are no monthly subscription fees for storage. You can stream movies to your TV, back up every device in your house, and access files remotely—all without paying a recurring bill.

This guide walks through the entire process: choosing hardware, installing software, configuring storage, and setting up remote access. No assumptions about prior server experience. Just practical steps that work.

Why Build a NAS Instead of Buying One?

Pre-built NAS units from Synology or QNAP are convenient. Plug in drives, click a few buttons, and you’re done. They also cost a premium. A 4-bay Synology enclosure with no drives runs around $400. For that same budget, you can build a machine with significantly more processing power, upgradeability, and storage capacity.

Building your own also means you’re not locked into proprietary software. If Synology decides to drop support for your model in three years, you’re stuck. With a DIY build, you can swap operating systems, upgrade components, or repurpose the hardware entirely.

The trade-off is time. You’ll spend an afternoon assembling and configuring. But once it’s running, maintenance is minimal.

Step 1: Choose Your Hardware

The “Just Works” Build

For most home users, this is the sweet spot. It handles file storage, media streaming, automated backups, and runs 24/7 without breaking the bank.

  • Case: Fractal Design Node 304 (mini-ITX, holds 6 drives)
  • Motherboard: ASRock B660M-ITX/ac (built-in WiFi is nice for initial setup)
  • CPU: Intel Core i3-12100 (efficient, has integrated graphics for transcoding)
  • RAM: 8GB DDR4 (start here, upgrade if you run virtual machines)
  • Power Supply: 300W-400W 80+ Bronze (don’t overspend, NAS draws little power)
  • Boot Drive: 120GB SATA SSD (for the operating system)
  • Storage Drives: Two 4TB WD Red Plus (NAS-rated, CMR technology)

Total cost: roughly $350-400 without storage drives. Add $100-120 per 4TB NAS drive.

The Budget Build

If you have an old desktop lying around, you can repurpose it. Minimum requirements:

  • Any dual-core CPU from the last 10 years
  • 4GB RAM (8GB recommended)
  • SATA ports for your drives (add a PCIe SATA card if needed)
  • A case that can hold at least two 3.5-inch drives

I started with a 2012 Dell Optiplex. It’s still running, serving files to five people without complaint.

What to Avoid

  • Raspberry Pi with USB drives: The USB bus is shared. One drive failing can corrupt the entire array. Also, USB drives aren’t designed for 24/7 operation.
  • Desktop hard drives (WD Blue, Seagate Barracuda): These don’t have TLER (Time-Limited Error Recovery). In a RAID array, a desktop drive might drop out unnecessarily, causing rebuild headaches.
  • Gaming power supplies: Overkill. A 1000W PSU running at 10% load is inefficient. Stick with 300-400W.

Step 2: Assemble the Hardware

This is straightforward. Mount the motherboard in the case, install the CPU and RAM, connect the power supply. For the storage drives:

  1. Install the boot SSD in any SATA port.
  2. Install your storage drives. If using a case like the Node 304, drives mount on their side with rubber grommets to reduce vibration.
  3. Connect SATA data cables to the motherboard and power cables from the PSU.

One tip: label your drives. Write “Boot”, “Drive 1”, “Drive 2” on masking tape and stick it on the cable. When a drive fails two years from now, you’ll thank yourself.

Step 3: Install the Operating System

TrueNAS Scale (Recommended)

TrueNAS Scale is free, open-source, and built on Linux. It supports ZFS, which is the gold standard for data integrity. It also runs Docker containers and virtual machines if you want to expand later.

  1. Download the TrueNAS Scale ISO from their website.
  2. Use BalenaEtcher or Rufus to write it to a USB stick (8GB or larger).
  3. Plug the USB into your NAS, boot from it.
  4. Follow the installer: select your boot SSD, set a root password, and let it install.
  5. After reboot, remove the USB installer. The system will boot from the SSD.
  6. Find the IP address shown on the monitor. Type that IP into a web browser on your main computer. You’ll see the TrueNAS web interface.

Alternative: Unraid

Unraid costs $59+ but offers easier drive expansion. You can mix drive sizes, add drives one at a time, and it has a huge community for app support. If you’re less technical and want something that “just works,” Unraid is worth the money.

I use TrueNAS because ZFS’s checksumming catches silent data corruption. Unraid doesn’t do that by default. For family photos and financial documents, I want that extra layer.

Step 4: Configure Your Storage Pool

In TrueNAS, storage is organized into pools. A pool is built from one or more virtual devices (vdevs). Each vdev can be a single drive, a mirror, or a RAID-Z array.

For Two Drives: Mirror

Two 4TB drives in a mirror gives you 4TB of usable space. If one drive fails, you replace it and the system rebuilds automatically. This is the simplest and most reliable setup for beginners.

In the TrueNAS web UI:

  1. Go to Storage → Create Pool.
  2. Name it “tank” (or anything).
  3. Drag both drives into the Data VDevs section.
  4. Select “Mirror” from the dropdown.
  5. Click Create.

For Three or More Drives: RAID-Z

RAID-Z is similar to RAID 5. With three 4TB drives, you get 8TB usable. One drive can fail without data loss. With four drives in RAID-Z2, you get 8TB usable but can lose two drives.

Choose RAID-Z if you need more capacity and can tolerate slightly more complexity during recovery.

Important: Don’t Fill Past 80%

ZFS performance degrades when a pool is over 80% full. Plan your capacity accordingly. If you need 6TB of storage, get drives that give you at least 7.5TB usable.

Step 5: Create Shares and Set Permissions

Now you need to make the storage accessible on your network.

For Windows/Mac/Linux: SMB Shares

  1. In TrueNAS, go to Shares → Windows (SMB) Shares → Add.
  2. Select the dataset (folder) you want to share.
  3. Enable “Allow Guest Access” only if you trust everyone on your network. Otherwise, create users under Accounts → Users and assign permissions.

For Time Machine Backups (Mac)

  1. Create a separate dataset just for Time Machine (e.g., “timemachine”).
  2. Enable the “Time Machine” flag in that dataset’s advanced options.
  3. In the SMB share settings, check “Enable Time Machine support.”

Now every Mac on your network will see the NAS as a backup destination. No more plugging in external drives.

Step 6: Set Up Remote Access (Securely)

This is where most people get it wrong. They forward port 443 or 80 to their NAS and call it done. That’s how you get ransomwared.

The Right Way: Tailscale

Tailscale creates a secure mesh VPN. You install it on your NAS and on your phone/laptop. All traffic goes through an encrypted tunnel. No ports open on your router.
